content: Bromide is a chemical compound that contains a bromide ion or ligand. A bromide ion consists of a bromine atom with an ionic charge of -1 (Br−). For instance, in cesium bromide (CsBr), cesium cations (Cs+) are electrically attracted to bromide anions (Br−), forming an electrically neutral ionic compound. The term bromide can also refer to a bromine atom with an oxidation number of -1 in covalent compounds, such as sulfur dibromide (SBr₂). Bromide ions are present in approximately 2% of all dissolved salts. Seafood and deep-sea plants typically have high levels of bromide, whereas land-derived foods contain variable amounts. To test for the presence of bromide ions, one can add excess dilute nitric acid (HNO₃) followed by a dilute aqueous solution of silver nitrate (AgNO₃). The formation of a creamy silver bromide precipitate confirms the presence of bromide ions. Bromide compounds, particularly potassium bromide, were widely used as sedatives in the 19th and early 20th centuries. In the United States, bromides were included in over-the-counter sedatives and headache remedies, such as Bromo-Seltzer, until 1975, when they were withdrawn due to concerns about chronic toxicity. This historical use contributed to the colloquial meaning of the word bromide as a dull or overused cliché, akin to a verbal sedative. The bromide ion has antiepileptic properties, and bromide salts are still used for this purpose, especially in veterinary medicine. Bromide ions are excreted by the kidneys, and their half-life in the human body is approximately 12 days, which is relatively long compared to many pharmaceuticals. This long half-life makes dosing adjustments challenging, as it may take several months for a new dose to reach equilibrium. Bromide ion concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid are about 30% of those in the blood and are significantly influenced by the body's chloride intake and metabolism. In the United States, bromide is still used in veterinary medicine, particularly for treating seizures in dogs. Veterinary diagnostic laboratories routinely measure blood bromide levels, as there are no FDA-approved uses for bromide in humans, and it is no longer available in over-the-counter sedatives. In some European countries, such as Germany, bromide is still used therapeutically for human epilepsy, and therapeutic bromide levels are measured. Chronic bromide toxicity can lead to a condition known as bromism, which is characterized by various neurological symptoms. Bromide toxicity can also cause a type of skin eruption. Potassium bromide and lithium bromide were historically used as sedatives, but their use declined in the mid-20th century due to the availability of safer and more effective alternatives, such as barbiturates. Lithium bromide was also used as a treatment for bipolar disorder, similar to lithium carbonate and lithium chloride. During World War I, it was rumored that British soldiers were given bromide to suppress sexual urges, but this claim lacks strong documentation and is considered an urban myth, as the sedative effects of bromide would have likely impaired military performance. In Lord Dunsany's 1919 play Fame and the Poet, a soldier is described as being given bromide as a sedative for nervous exhaustion and overwork. In biology, bromine (in the form of bromide) has been identified as an essential cofactor for the peroxidasin-catalyzed formation of sulfilimine crosslinks in collagen IV. This post-translational modification occurs in all animals, making bromine an essential trace element for humans. Bromide is also required by eosinophils, a type of white blood cell specialized for combating multicellular parasites. Eosinophils use bromide to generate antiparasitic brominating compounds, such as hypobromite, through the action of eosinophil peroxidase, a haloperoxidase enzyme that can use chloride but preferentially utilizes bromide when available. Beyond its role in collagen IV production and its facultative use by eosinophils, bromide is not known to be essential for other animal life functions, as its roles can generally be replaced by chloride, albeit less effectively in some cases. Land plants do not utilize bromide. Bromide salts are sometimes used in hot tubs and spas as mild germicidal agents. In these settings, an added oxidizing agent generates hypobromite in situ, mimicking the peroxidase activity in eosinophils. Bromide may be a minor but necessary nutrient for collagen IV-producing marine animals. Some sea animals, such as Murex snails, use bromide to synthesize organic compounds. Bromide ions are also heavily concentrated by certain species of ocean algae, which use them to produce methyl bromide and a variety of brominated organic compounds. These reactions are catalyzed by unusual enzymes called vanadium bromoperoxidases. Bromide concentrations in human blood are influenced by dietary intake, particularly from seafood, as bromide is present in relatively high concentrations in seawater and many types of seafood.
